posts.note: 42-word podcast blurb that re-creates the prior article; no forward-looking statements.
Rerun of an older Auvelity (dextromethorphan/bupropion) explainer. Describes the FDA approval and label claims in past or present tense; no forward-looking calls by the author found.

The satirical value-based care vendor pitch ('We promise to save you money') is not logged: the author's point is that such savings are regression to the mean, so the pitch does not read as a sincere expectation.
Body is a guest narrative by clinical trial participant Jonathan Rosenberg. His past beliefs about relapse are his own, past-tense, and not logged as the author's forecasts.

statements.quote: It's possible, for example, that there is inflammatory depression as a subtype that might be relevant for whether someone will respond to transcranial magnetic stimulation as delivered in this setting
statements.context: Discussion of Koparal et al. (2025), a retrospective study of 86 treatment-resistant depression patients at Gazi University (Ankara) that links a high neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) to non-response to 10 Hz rTMS. The author floats the hypothesis that an inflammatory depression subtype exists and could predict who responds to rTMS.
statements.note: Borderline: a scientific hypothesis about a present state (a subtype exists), not a dated call. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: This is potentially a big-deal finding, and it should be replicated—which I'm writing this article to suggest somebody do.
statements.context: Closing evaluation of the Koparal et al. (2025) finding that NLR (odds ratio 0.373) accounts for about 7% of the variance in rTMS response. The author calls it potentially a big-deal finding and urges replication.
statements.note: Compound: a hedged significance call ('potentially a big-deal finding') plus advice to replicate ('should be replicated'). Mostly normative; weak predictive reading.

statements.quote: I'm adding another edition of Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment , my live in-person newsletter event, to the lineup, this time happening May 18 in Los Angeles!
statements.context: 'Plugs and Promotions' section at the end of the post. The author announces a new edition of his live in-person event, Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment (RAMHT), to take place May 18 in Los Angeles. Post dated 2025-03-17, so May 18, 2025 is implied.
statements.note: Event announcement for the author's own organization (RAMHT); a later coder marks CONTROL.

statements.quote: there is a fiduciary duty to uphold , and the time for scams is over.
statements.context: Closing line of a math think piece. The author sketches a satirical value-based care vendor that enrolls the top 1% of claimants, does nothing, and claims the savings that regression to the mean produces the next year. He then argues that Bayesian reasoning lets payers see through such pitches and declares the time for such scams over.
statements.note: Borderline: a rhetorical declaration, not a dated forecast. Reads as an expectation that payers stop paying for regression-to-the-mean 'savings'. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: However, where there is neurocircuitry, TMS researchers will soon find a way to modulate it.
statements.context: After listing the negative symptoms of schizophrenia (apathy, anhedonia, asociality, avolition, alogia, affective flattening) and noting that abulia has its own neurocircuitry, the author predicts TMS researchers will soon find ways to modulate that circuitry. He credits colleagues Shan Siddiqi, Mike Fox, David Carreon, Nolan Williams and Deepak Sarpal.
statements.note: General call about the pace of TMS research on negative-symptom neurocircuitry.

statements.quote: Today’s article focuses on two new lines of evidence that suggest this brain circuit approach may be promising for schizophrenia
statements.context: Setup for the article. Two RCTs: Han et al. (Brain Stimulation, March 19, 2025), accelerated personalised iTBS targeting the left prefrontal region most connected to the VTA for negative symptoms (n=80, Cohen's d 0.83 at week 4); and an earlier RCT for positive symptoms (auditory hallucinations, AHRS). The author says the brain circuit (TMS) approach may be promising for schizophrenia.
statements.note: Hedged; 'promising' carries an expectation about future evidence and adoption rather than a dated call.

statements.quote: So, with luck, in just over 20 years, these evidence-based treatments will be subject to the same absurd and degrading process for prior authorization demanded by UnitedHealth Group for OCD and Depression we love today…if it feels closer than ever!
statements.context: After stating that RCT data now support TMS approaches to both positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia, the author sarcastically forecasts that payer coverage of TMS for schizophrenia, with prior authorization as UnitedHealth Group requires for OCD and depression, will take roughly 20 years to arrive. He then suggests readers call their congressperson or health plan.
statements.note: Sarcastic framing. Underlying claim reads sincere: payer coverage of TMS for schizophrenia will lag the evidence by decades and come with prior authorization.

statements.quote: That is the end of part II! Stay tuned for the final chapter in this three part tale tomorrow!
statements.context: Closing line of part II of a three-part guest series by clinical trial participant Jonathan Rosenberg about his depression and an accelerated TMS (H1 coil) trial in which the author was PI. It announces that part III will publish the next day (post dated 2025-03-24).
statements.note: Newsletter's own publication schedule (author's own organization). The closing line may be editorial (Owen) or Jon's; treated as the author's.
